newsitem.title: PERU: Peru urges Japanese firms not to pay ransom.
newsitem.headline: Peru urges Japanese firms not to pay ransom.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori urged Japanese firms on Wednesday not to pay ransoms to Marxist guerrillas holding their representatives among the 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
"I hope that these companies do not give in to their pressures," Fujimori told reporters as the hostage crisis entered its fourth week.
Earlier, Peru and Japan turned their wrath on journalists, accusing them of jeopardising efforts to end the deadlock.

At the centre of the controversy were a reporter and a translator working for Japanese television station TV Asahi, who sneaked past police on Tuesday for a two-hour meeting with Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.

Peruvian anti-terrorism police detained the pair and confiscated their notebooks and cameras as they came out of the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence. Authorities were deciding whether to press charges against them, police sources said on Wednesday.

Fujimori, who has repeatedly said he would stand firm against "blackmail from the terrorists" demanding the release of about 400 comrades, told CNN in an interview on Wednesday: "We are waiting for a favourable condition for beginning again the talks" with the MRTA.

Fujimori ruled out peace talks with the MRTA during or after the hostage crisis and added that he would not use force against the hostage-takers as long as the captives were not hurt, according to CNN.
In a visit to a Lima shantytown on Wednesday Fujimori told a crowd: "We are not going to allow the terrorists to continue killing."

Referring to the Japanese reporter who sneaked into the ambassador's residence, Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, speaking on a tour of Southeast Asian nations, said the reporter could have harmed efforts to solve the crisis.

"It is very regrettable," a Foreign Ministry official quoted Hashimoto as saying. "An act like that could create unforeseeable circumstances and disrupt the Peruvian government's efforts for a peaceful resolution and the release of all hostages."
TV Asahi named the two as Peruvian interpreter Victor Borja and New York-based reporter Tsuyoshi Hitomi.

The pair's entry into the residence, as well as the entry on New Year's Eve by a larger group of journalists, was also condemned by Peruvian Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi as "damaging to the seriousness and fluidity of talks."
The action was an embarrassment for police, who immediately tightened security around the residence.

"Once again, the incompetence of the Peruvian police has been shown to the whole world," wrote political commentator Manuel D'Ornellas in the daily Expreso. "For the second time in a few days, Japanese journalists managed to mock the cordon supposedly surrounding the building."

Local media reported two suspected MRTA members or supporters were arrested outside the ambassador's residence on Wednesday. Also reported arrested were the owners of a house through which the Asahi pair entered the ambassador's compound.
The MRTA rebels stormed the residence on Dec. 17 and took about 500 hostages including ambassadors and senior Peruvian government officials. Most of them were later released.
The guerrillas have said they will stay in the residence as long as necessary to secure their principal demand, the release of about 400 jailed comrades.

"We have all the time in the world. The question is if the personalities inside are prepared to bear that. It is up to the government to take the necessary steps for an early exchange of prisoners," said MRTA international spokesman Isaac Velazco in a telephone interview from Hamburg.
"We do not know the word surrender," he added.

Beatriz Boza, head of the government's public relations unit Promperu, told reporters that despite the crisis, Peru had received a total $1.5 billion in foreign investment and loans since the Dec. 17 takeover.
"Those are figures that show that the theme of investor confidence and credit ... has not been affected," she said.
